headline: Agaru is from Old Japanese, first attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE.
Nagame is the continuative stem of 眺める (nagameru, “to gaze at”).
Tsuchi is first attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE.
Ichiji is 一 (ichi, “one”) plus 時 (ji), either “o'clock” or “time”.
Mibun appears to be a shift from older shinbun, swapping the on'yomi shin for the kun'yomi mi; first attested in 1688.
Hōki is an alteration of hahaki, first cited to a text from 1496.
Ijō is an orthographic borrowing from Chinese 以上 (yǐshàng).
Senchi is borrowed from French centi-, possibly via English centi-.
Kasokudo is 加 (“add, increase”) plus 速度 (“speed, velocity”).
Dekiru began as ideku in the Man'yōshū of 759, written 出で来.
Nettai is from Literary Chinese 熱帶 (rèdài, literally “heat, high temperature + belt, zone, area”), coined by missionaries in China.
Saikin is 最 (sai-, “most”) plus 近 (kin, “close”).
Uwasa originally referred to private conversation about one's social superiors, and is possibly from 上 (ufa, “up, upward”).
Monosugoi is 物 (mono-, “somehow; very”) plus 凄い (sugoi, “terrible; amazing”).
Yappari is the emphatic pronunciation of やはり (yahari).
Omae is literally “honourable presence in front of me”, originally a polite pronoun for emperors or gods, first attested in the early 900s.
Tan'i is from Middle Chinese 單位 (tan hwijᴴ).
Mechakucha's etymology is hypothetical: 無茶 (mucha) shifted to 滅茶 (mecha) by ateji.
Bideo is called an internationalism; see English video.
Hisshi is 必 (hitsu, “necessary”) plus 死 (shi, “death”).
Noseru, “to take on board”, is cognate with 載せる (noseru), from the Classical Japanese verb のす (nosu).
Ippan is Middle Chinese 一般, literally “one + sort”.
Sakan is a sound shift from 盛り (sakari), sharing a root with 栄える (sakaeru, “to thrive”) and 咲く (saku, “to bloom”).
Saraishū is analyzed as either 再来 (sarai, “two next”) plus 週, or 再 (sa, “again”) plus 来週 (raishū); first attested in 1966.
Sentā is borrowed from English center, centre.
Musume is analyzed as 生す (musu, “to beget”) plus 女 (me, “female”).
Genshō is from Middle Chinese 現象 (MC henH zjangX).
Shoho is from Middle Chinese 初步.
Masumasu is a reduplication of 増す (masu).
Shikashi is possibly a shift from 然り (shikari, “being like so”) plus し.
Kōkōsei is 高校 (kōkō, “high school”) plus 生 (-sei, “student; pupil”).
